In democratic societies, everyone has *some* responsibility on how the use of technology maximizes benefits and minimizes bad side effects. The benefits of AI are real today, and will greatly expand in the future. The bad side effects have, so far, been minimal. It's on all of us to make sure it remains that way. The catastrophe scenarios (extinction, employment apocalypse, etc) are totally ridiculous for anyone who understands how thing work in the real world. And the p(doom) estimates are all pulled out of their authors' back ends. It makes no sense to attribute a probability to events over which we have complete agency. Whatever probability you come up with merely reveals your lack of confidence that your fellow humans will do the right thing. Confidence in humanity is one thing Geoff and I disagree on. The other thing we disagree on is the primacy of intelligence. In the real world, intelligence is not synonymous with power and dominance. A virus, a poisonous snake, or a tiger can bring down a human. Lots of very stupid humans dominate much smarter ones (just look at the international political scene). Superintelligent AI will work for us and do our bidding, subject to safety guardrails. It will have no desire to take over. I have made detailed technical proposals for AI architectures that can be made safe by satisfying safety guardrails at inference time. I call it Objective-Driven AI Architecture.

When I asked for sources, Claude replied: "what the recreation was built from: SpaceX’s official webcast replay of Flight 15 (YouTube): seconds 74 to 116 drive the timing, camera shots and catch moment, and it’s the footage in the side-by-side and the comparison video. Wikipedia’s “SpaceX Starship (spacecraft)” article: the ship’s layout for the blueprint view, including tanks, header tanks, downcomers, pressure bottles and engines. Guinness World Records: the 146 m tower height. Community cut-away drawings: which way the tank domes bulge. Everything else is estimated, including heights along the hull, tank sizes, pipe routing and catch rail height. No SpaceX engineering drawings were used."

BREAKING: Samsung reportedly plans to make chips for SpaceX’s Starlink satellites in Austin, Texas. Samsung is investing $1.9 billion to expand its Austin chip factory, with the planned operations targeted to begin by 2030, according to Seoul Economic Daily. The chip, called STM32V8, is already used in Starlink’s mini laser system. SpaceX’s Starlink engineering team has praised the chip’s performance. The chips are currently manufactured in France. The reported Texas plan would add American production capacity for a key component behind Starlink’s satellite communications.

This thought came from a simple harness I have been trying to build that more natively encodes all these important deterministic components with my agents (e.g., mixing Jev classifier and verification tools with coding agents). I am just tired of all these harnesses that try to automate everything and end up inviting more issues down the road. The state of harnesses has been really bad more recently (with the exception of a few). Plus, more people want to create software factories and complain about all kinds of issues showing up during complex runs. I feel like we still have a lot of work to do on harnesses. Excited to keep experimenting, but I wanted to share how I feel, because I think a lot of people believe that "coding is solved" and mistake that for meaning you can just put your agents to ship code in auto mode.

Samsung will invest $1.9 billion to expand its chip plant in Austin, Texas, to produce semiconductors for @SpaceX's Starlink satellites. The factory is expected to produce STM32V8 chips used in Starlink's laser communication systems, shifting production currently based in France to the U.S. The chips use an advanced 18nm FD-SOI process designed for high performance, low power consumption, and durability in harsh space environments. Production is targeted to begin by 2030, according to the Seoul Economic Daily.
